# The Art of Noticing

In an age that treats attention as a currency to be mined, the simple act of noticing has become a quiet rebellion. Every day, we walk through a world saturated with detail—the particular slant of afternoon light on a brick wall, the way a stranger adjusts their glasses, the faint smell of rain before the first drop falls—and yet most of it passes through us unregistered. We are too busy, too distracted, too caught in the endless scroll of other people’s lives to notice the one unfolding right in front of us. To notice is not merely to see; it is to pause, to allow the world to impress itself upon us, and in doing so, to remember that we are alive.

I first understood this on an ordinary Tuesday morning. I was walking to the train station, earbuds in, mentally rehearsing the day’s tasks, when a flash of movement made me look up. A small bird—a sparrow, perhaps—had landed on a branch just above my head. It was not doing anything remarkable. It tilted its head, ruffled its feathers, and then flew off. But for a fraction of a second, I was entirely there. The sound of traffic receded. The list of emails waiting in my inbox lost its urgency. In that brief moment, the world felt larger than my anxieties, and I felt less like a machine executing tasks and more like a person participating in a vast, ongoing mystery.

This is the paradox of noticing: it requires us to slow down in a culture that equates speed with competence. We are taught from an early age to be productive, to fill every spare moment with something useful. Idleness is suspect. Daydreaming is a waste. Yet the most meaningful experiences often arrive precisely when we are not trying to accomplish anything—when we are simply present enough to receive them. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it.” The order is important. Attention comes first. Astonishment follows. Telling about it is secondary. But without the first step, the other two remain impossible.

What does it mean to pay attention? It is not the same as focusing on a screen, which often narrows our awareness to a single glowing rectangle while the rest of the world fades. True attention is expansive. It is a kind of openness, a willingness to be interrupted by reality. The philosopher Simone Weil called attention “the rarest and purest form of generosity.” To attend to someone—or something—is to offer it the gift of your full presence. It is to say, without words, “You matter enough for me to set aside my own preoccupations and simply look.” In a world of fragmented glances and half-listened conversations, such attention feels almost radical.

Noticing is also deeply tied to memory. I can recall with startling clarity the color of the sky on a particular evening ten years ago, the way the clouds were streaked with orange and pink like oil on water. But I cannot remember what I ate for lunch three days ago. The difference is attention. One moment was witnessed; the other was merely consumed. Attention is what transforms experience into memory, what turns the raw data of the senses into something we carry with us. When we fail to notice, we live in a kind of amnesia, accumulating days that vanish without leaving a trace.

There is also an ethical dimension to noticing. The writer David Foster Wallace, in his famous commencement speech “This Is Water,” argued that the real value of education is learning how to choose what to pay attention to. He described the mundane frustrations of adult life—traffic jams, long grocery lines, crowded parking lots—and suggested that we have a choice in how we interpret them. We can see other people as obstacles in our way, or we can remember that each of them is carrying a burden we cannot see. Noticing, in this sense, is not just an aesthetic practice but a moral one. It is the foundation of empathy. We cannot care about what we do not see.

Yet noticing is difficult. Our environment is engineered to distract us. Notifications ping like needy children. Algorithms learn our weaknesses and exploit them. The average person now checks their phone hundreds of times a day, often without conscious intention. Each glance is a small act of attention withdrawn from the physical world and invested in a virtual one. The result is a pervasive sense of what the sociologist Hartmut Rosa calls “social acceleration”—the feeling that life is speeding up even as our ability to savor it diminishes. We are everywhere and nowhere, connected to everyone and present to no one.

How do we reclaim the art of noticing? It does not require a retreat to a monastery or a digital detox that lasts for months. It can begin with something as simple as a walk without headphones. Or a meal eaten without the accompaniment of a screen. Or a deliberate pause before entering a room to observe what is actually there: the quality of light, the arrangement of objects, the expressions on people’s faces. The painter Georgia O’Keeffe once said, “Nobody sees a flower really; it is so small. We haven’t time, and to see takes time—like to have a friend takes time.” Noticing requires time, but not necessarily large quantities of it. It requires only that we stop treating time as a resource to be optimized and start treating it as a medium for living.

One practice I have found helpful is what I call “the sensory inventory.” At random moments throughout the day, I pause and silently name five things I can see, four things I can hear, three things I can feel, two things I can smell, and one thing I can taste. It is a simple exercise, almost childlike, but it reliably pulls me out of the spiral of rumination and back into the present. I have noticed that the world is always offering itself to us—in the rustle of leaves, the warmth of a coffee cup, the distant sound of a train, the faint saltiness of the air near the sea. The problem is not that life lacks richness; the problem is that we are so often absent from it.

There is a special relationship between noticing and writing. To write well, one must first observe well. The writer’s task is to render the familiar strange, to find the exact word for that particular shade of blue, to capture the texture of a moment before it slips away. Many of my own ideas begin not as grand concepts but as small observed details: a woman crying quietly on a park bench, a child walking backward to keep his shadow behind him, a plastic bag caught in a tree like a tattered flag. These details are the raw material of storytelling. They remind us that the universal is found in the particular, that the meaning of life is not hidden in some distant abstraction but embedded in the ordinary, if only we have eyes to see.

Ultimately, noticing is a form of love. To notice something is to affirm its existence, to grant it a place in your consciousness. And what we notice, we tend to protect. The environmentalist Baba Dioum wrote, “In the end we will conserve only what we love; we will love only what we understand; and we will understand only what we are taught.” But before understanding, before love, there must be attention. We cannot love a world we have never truly seen. We cannot grieve the loss of something we never noticed was there.

So I am trying to notice more. I am trying to look up from my phone when I walk, to listen without planning my response, to let my eyes linger on the ordinary until it becomes extraordinary. It is not easy. There are days when I slip back into the fog of distraction, when hours pass and I cannot account for them. But I keep returning to the practice, because attention is the only way I know to be fully alive. The world is offering itself to us at every moment, quietly, persistently, without demand. All we have to do is notice.
